new_statements.translation: [2021] In Xipaya, the symbol ´ over the vowel indicates the phonological accent; it is absent here when the word is oxytone (final-stressed). Unlike Juruna, which has a tonal opposition, Xipaya marks no difference of tone. [2008] In the cognate table the acute accent marks, in Xipaya, the stressed syllable when it is not the last syllable. [2008 n.8] The analysis presented is based on Carmen Rodrigues (1990). [Nimuendajú] The stress sometimes seems evenly distributed over the various syllables; in other cases, however, it is placed sharply on a single vowel and is then marked with ´.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Xipaya has phonemic ('phonological') word accent and no tone; final (oxytone) stress is the unmarked/default case and non-final stress must be lexically marked. In the authors' 296-item cognate list about three quarters of Xipaya forms are unmarked (final stress) and about one quarter carry a marked penult (occasionally antepenult), e.g. úpata 'ripen', ánï 'that', yáhu 'stingray', -séba 'wing', etúku 'eat (intr.)' vs. apï 'dog', aka 'house', pïza 'canoe'.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as such; Nimuendajú notes the collective plural -ĭ retracting the accent of the loan karaí > karái. (Observation from the 2008 cognate list, not an authorial claim: many penult-marked forms end in recurrent formatives -ku, -pa, -hu, so root-final stress with unstressed suffixes is a possible underlying generalisation that only Rodrigues 1990/1995 could confirm.)
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, isolated lexical (citation) forms in phonological transcription; statement is a transcription convention plus the label 'acento fonológico', not a full accent chapter. The full analysis is in Rodrigues 1990 (unpublished DEA mémoire, Paris 7), which the 2008 paper names as its basis.
new_statements.identity_note: All modern statements rest on Carmen Rodrigues's data from essentially one speaker (Iawaidu, Altamira, PA; recordings from 1988 on), analysis based on Rodrigues 1990. Nimuendajú 1923-24 describes 'Šipáia' as spoken c. 1916-1919 (same language, xipa1240). The sister language Juruna/Yudjá (juru1256) is tonal with tone-driven accent; the same authors state Xipaya has no tone.
